current_text.html: Ministers Transferring into the Presbytery a. A Minister seeking admission to a Presbytery from another Presbytery in the Presbyterian Church in America shall be examined on Christian experience (including personal character and family management), and also as to his views in theology, the Sacraments, and church government. If the examining Presbytery does not accept the Minister seeking admission, it shall record this fact along with its rationale, if one is adopted, in the minutes, and shall communicate its rationale to his current Presbytery. b. If an applicant comes from another denomination, the Presbytery shall examine him thoroughly as required by the trials listed in BCO 21-4 and require him to answer in the affirmative the questions put to candidates at their ordination. Ordained ministers from other denominations being considered by Presbyteries for reception may come under the extraordinary provisions set forth in BCO 21-4. c. In every case, Presbyteries shall require each ordained minister entering the Presbytery to state the specific instances in which he may differ with the Confession of Faith and Catechisms in any of their statements and/or propositions, which differences the court shall judge in accordance with BCO 21-4.f-g (see also RAO 16-3.e.7.a-d).

metadata.synopsis: Heritage Presbytery treated a member's September 2016 filing against her session as a BCO 43-3 complaint and began adjudicating it. The SJC sustained RE Scott Dailey's complaint against that action. BCO 43-3 allows higher-court review only if the lower court denies a complaint or fails to consider it by its next stated meeting. The session timely ruled the filing did not meet BCO 43-1 and did consider it, so neither condition applied. Presbytery's post-November 12, 2016 adjudicative actions were annulled; possible underlying disciplinary matters were left to BCO 31-2 and 40-5.

metadata.synopsis: Ministers complained that Southwest Florida Presbytery improperly reexamined Bryan Gregory and reversed his examination, membership, and call after previously receiving him. The SJC upheld Presbytery’s authority to hear and sustain the earlier complaint but sustained the present complaint on the remedial actions. Sustaining a complaint did not itself undo prior acts; once Presbytery had treated Gregory as a member, his membership rights could be removed only through disciplinary due process. The SJC annulled the reexamination and March 24 actions and directed Presbytery to consider appropriate remedies. Gregory’s theology was not before it.

metadata.synopsis: Louisiana Presbytery’s refusal to institute process after examining Steve Wilkins’s Federal Vision teachings was challenged for applying the wrong constitutional standard and overlooking a strong presumption that some views were out of conformity with the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s denial. The ruling did not adjudicate Wilkins’s guilt; the Central Carolina memorial remained before the SJC.
